overview: This file brings together U.S. consular reporting and State Department routing material concerning agriculture in Japanese-ruled Taiwan in 1940. Its principal documents are a Shanghai transmittal and an enclosed memorandum by Agricultural Attaché Owen L. Dawson describing the value of his fact-finding trip, the cooperation of Taiwanese specialists, and severe military restrictions on agricultural data, followed by Consul Gerald Warner’s detailed report that typhoons, fertilizer shortages, insects, and wartime demands had made 1940 an exceptionally poor agricultural year. Warner discusses disappointing rice and sugar production, widespread damage to other crops, likely concealment of unfavorable statistics, and the prospect of tighter rationing for the Formosan Chinese population while exports continued to Japan. The bundle concludes with two brief departmental routing memoranda whose precise relationship to the agricultural reports is not fully evident from the surviving pages.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Dawson’s memorandum on agricultural conditions in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Richard P. Butrick, American Consul, Shanghai
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Butrick transmits Agricultural Attaché Owen L. Dawson’s memorandum on conditions encountered during an official trip to Taiwan via Japan.
subfiles.summary: The covering despatch forwards Dawson’s memorandum of May 7, 1940, which contains significant observations from his recent official journey to Taiwan. Copies were sent to the Department of State and the Department of Agriculture.

subfiles.title: Dawson memorandum on his official agricultural trip to Taiwan
subfiles.from: Owen L. Dawson, American Agricultural Attaché
subfiles.to: American Consulate General, Shanghai; transmitted to the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Dawson assesses the information gathered, professional contacts made, and official obstacles encountered during his agricultural investigation in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Dawson reports collecting substantial material for a future study of Taiwanese agriculture, although some Japanese-language sources still required translation and analysis. Taiwanese specialists were cordial, but military rules barred release of the latest two years of statistics and sometimes older basic data, greatly limiting his investigation. He contrasts these restrictions with the relatively free access then available in Japan Proper and suggests seeking reciprocal access to Japanese agricultural research in exchange for information obtained from the United States and the Philippines. He praises the assistance of the American consul and the Taihoku consulate’s interpreter, Matsuo.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on poor agricultural production in Taiwan in 1940
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Warner reports that typhoons, fertilizer shortages, and insect damage had frustrated efforts to increase Taiwanese agricultural production in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Warner predicts that 1940 will be one of Taiwan’s poorest agricultural years in recent memory and warns that official statistics may conceal the extent of the failure. Rice production fell well short of Tokyo’s target, while estimates for the sugar crop were repeatedly reduced after the August 30 and September 29–30 typhoons. Cotton and numerous other crops—including cassava, bananas, sweet potatoes, fruit, sugar cane, rice, tobacco, jute, ramie, and castor beans—also suffered serious losses. Warner concludes that the prolonged China Incident had compounded these problems and that rationing of the Formosan Chinese population would probably become more severe as Japanese needs received priority.

subfiles.title: Trade Agreements Division routing sheet concerning possible Treasury consultation
subfiles.from: Unidentified Department of State officials, including H. S.
subfiles.about: Departmental officials discuss whether Treasury should be consulted and whether a consulate should simply be told to keep the Department informed.
subfiles.summary: A July 16 annotation asks whether the matter should be checked with Treasury and, if Treasury agrees, whether the consulate should be advised that no action is required beyond continued reporting. A July 25 reply records a conversation with Mr. Corkhill and indicates that a communication or instruction to the consulate had been drafted, although the OCR is unclear. The underlying despatch or issue is not identified on this page.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum referring a consular despatch for consideration
subfiles.from: Department of State, Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs; Jones and M. H. P.
subfiles.to: FA, an internal Department of State office
subfiles.about: The Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs calls another office’s attention to a despatch and particularly to Consul Warner’s request in its final paragraph.
subfiles.summary: This short internal memorandum recommends that “FA” consider an unspecified despatch, especially Consul Warner’s request in its last paragraph. The referenced despatch is not clearly identifiable from this page and does not appear to be Warner’s October 4 agricultural report, whose final paragraph contains no explicit request.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how Japanese military secrecy constrained American collection of even ostensibly civilian agricultural statistics in colonial Taiwan. Dawson’s account documents the asymmetry between Japanese access to American and Philippine research and the limited access granted to foreign investigators, while Warner’s later report supplies unusually detailed estimates of crop targets, typhoon losses, and likely official manipulation of published figures. Together the reports connect environmental disaster, wartime mobilization, colonial export priorities, and food rationing; the out-of-sequence July and October material also illustrates how related documents and routing slips accumulated within State Department decimal files.
